title: Free-GPU Video Production
topic: luke. at the aiquest channel and yeah give me like
subtitle: How to generate AI video end to end on free cloud GPUs — picking a MiniMax H3 distillation variant, running the dual-T4 notebook, diagnosing the failures that only show up at 480p, bolting long-term character memory onto an open backbone with StoryMem, and knowing the exact moment the free tier stops being enough. Distilled from AIQUEST's two open-video-model teardowns, with the fine-tuning, eval and deployment practice around them drawn from Fahd Mirza, Zen van Riel, Sebastian Raschka, Dave Ebbelaar, LangChain, Ray Fu, Gaurav Sen and others.
question: Can you Luke. At the AIQuest channel And, yeah, give me, like, a rundown on what's happening, you know, like, especially focusing on mini max h three. I wanna, like, get into the process of building or, you know, experience building, like, a AI video. End to end. So, you know, I wanna start and just get a feel for the models and, like, the variants, especially AI Quest channel shows like, how to simplify or how to make those models have long and short term memory. So I wanna implement that with my video. But, yeah, I wanna start with the base case. Tell me you know, what stage one just running on Google Colab and then you know, if I wanted... Could I keep using Google Colab to generate videos, or will I need to pivot somewhere else?

sources.title: Fine-Tune Qwen3.5 0.8B Locally On Your Own Dataset - Full Easy Guide
sources.contributed: A full, parameter-by-parameter walkthrough of LoRA fine-tuning a small local model (unsloth + TRL SFTTrainer) on a 200-row custom dataset, with concrete hyperparameter values and before/after output comparison.

sources.title: Build a Full-Stack GenAI Project in 4 Hours (FastAPI, React, Supabase)
sources.contributed: A monorepo full-stack RAG build (FastAPI + React + Supabase + pgvector) for a hypothetical client, showing agents.md-driven setup, hybrid retrieval with agentic tool loops, grounding/citation validators, and a Railway deployment.

sources.title: Building Better AI Agents: Artificial Intelligence Observability How To
sources.contributed: Frames agent observability (runs/traces/threads) as the prerequisite infrastructure that powers every type of agent eval, and shows LangChain's internal workflow for mining Terminal-Bench traces to improve their deep-agents coding harness.

sources.title: Complete Beginner's Course on AI Evaluations in 50 Minutes (2025) | Aman Khan
sources.contributed: Walks a full live example of building a customer-support-agent eval pipeline end to end — prompt, human-labeled rubric/spreadsheet, LLM-as-judge, and match-rate validation — using Anthropic's console and the Arise platform.

sources.title: Complete Guide to building an AI Trading Bot with Claude for Beginners
sources.contributed: Shows a concrete non-technical workflow for having Claude Code build and schedule a working moving-average-crossover trading bot wired to Alpaca's paper-trading API via MCP.

sources.title: Build a Complete End-to-End GenAI Project in 3 Hours
sources.contributed: A single-person, single-repo AI news aggregator build (scrapers to database to agents to email to render deployment) that shows the moment-to-moment prompting and architectural-decision loop with a coding agent.

sources.title: Agentic AI made me an 100x engineer!
sources.contributed: A 30-year open-source/Linux driver maintainer's first-person log of four weeks using Claude (Pro then Max plan) to resurrect dozens of decades-dead hardware drivers, with real token/dollar cost figures and a skeptical, 'LLMs are a dead end for AGI' framing that cuts against typical AI-hype talks.

sources.title: How to make an $8K/month Youtube Channel with Claude
sources.contributed: Lays out a five-step faceless-YouTube production pipeline (niche selection by RPM data, scripting rules, voice cloning, three tiers of AI visuals) built almost entirely around Claude prompts.

sources.title: MiniMax H3 is Now Crazy Fast (Free Kaggle Notebook)
sources.contributed: Head-to-head benchmark of three 4-step distillation LoRAs (PDMD, DMAD, Fused Turbo) for the MiniMax H3 video model, plus exact steps and specs for running it free on dual Kaggle T4 GPUs.

sources.title: Design with AI - Full Guide (Tools, Workflows, Design Systems)
sources.contributed: Head-to-head token/time/quality comparison of AI design tools (Grok, Claude Fable/Opus, Codex, Figma AI, Google Stitch, cursor) and a staged workflow (iterate -> prototype/QA -> align to design system) using different tools for each stage.

sources.title: How I Build and Ship Custom AI Solutions for Clients
sources.contributed: The agency-level process: discovery, scoping into PoC vs MVP, proposal structure, two-week sprint cadence and pricing, the standardized Genai Launchpad stack, and the Hetzner/Caddy/Langfuse/Sentry deployment and monitoring setup.

sources.title: 20 AI Concepts Explained in 40 Minutes
sources.contributed: A compact glossary-style map of the full LLM concept stack (tokens, vectors, attention, self-supervised learning, transformers, fine-tuning, RAG, MCP, context engineering, agents, RLHF, chain-of-thought, SLMs/distillation, quantization) that the other three talks assume as background.

sources.title: The Best AI Automation Stack to Learn in 2026
sources.contributed: A concrete five-layer custom-code stack (Python/FastAPI/Celery, Postgres/Supabase, React/Vite/shadcn, model APIs, Docker/Railway/Hetzner) as the alternative to no-code automation tools.

sources.title: Build an LLM from Scratch 7: Instruction Finetuning
sources.contributed: Code-level walkthrough of building an instruction-tuning dataset, collate function, padding/masking, and using a local LLM (Ollama) as an automated judge to score fine-tuned responses.

sources.title: How to Systematically Setup LLM Evals (Metrics, Unit Tests, LLM-as-a-Judge)
sources.contributed: A dedicated framework for the three levels of LLM evals (unit tests, human+LLM-judge, A/B testing), the analyze-measure-improve loop, and the human/LLM alignment process with concrete agreement-score tooling.

sources.title: The Honest Guide To Fine-Tuning Local AI In 2026
sources.contributed: A decision framework for when to fine-tune vs. prompt/RAG/agentic loops, plus concrete hardware, VRAM, and time benchmarks for local LoRA fine-tuning.

sources.title: Minute Long AI Story Videos With Consistent Characters? Meet StoryMem
sources.contributed: Explains ByteDance's StoryMem LoRA — the memory-bank mechanism (negative RoPE shift, CLIP + HPSv3 keyframe filtering) that lets any Wan 2.2-based video model hold character consistency across minute-long, multi-scene stories, with exact training/parameter/VRAM figures.

sources.title: Learn Design Systems: Figma Variables, Components, AI, and More
sources.contributed: From-scratch teaching of design token tiering (brand/alias/mapped), component variant structure, and the specific skills-based workaround needed because AI cannot reliably sync with or build a design system on its own.

sources.title: The Never Ending Lore of Harness | Vivek Trivedy (Product Lead, Langchain)
sources.contributed: A practitioner's definition and operating playbook for 'agent harnesses' — prompting, verification, orchestration, file systems, context rot mitigation, continual learning, and when to reach for RL vs. context engineering — from LangChain's open-source agent lead.

sources.title: RFT, DPO, SFT: Fine-tuning with OpenAI — Ilan Bigio, OpenAI
sources.contributed: The only non-AIQUEST, non-video-gen talk in this cluster: a live, code-heavy walkthrough of OpenAI's three fine-tuning methods, when each one fits, concrete data-volume thresholds, and two on-stage failures (RFT email classifier, live 'prompt tuning' experiment).

gaps: This cluster bundles four unrelated videos on different topics (OpenAI fine-tuning APIs, two AIQUEST video-generation tool reviews, and a personal essay on agentic coding for retro Linux drivers) with no shared throughline — a reader expecting a coherent 'Luke at AIQUEST' guide won't find one from these four sources alone; only rEjasJZq1t8 and GM70MDyl94E are actually AIQUEST videos.
None of the videos state the dollar cost of OpenAI fine-tuning jobs (training compute price, per-token inference price for a fine-tuned model) — JfaLQqfXqPA never gives pricing.
The RFT grader-design guidance stays qualitative ('does it benefit from more accuracy') with no worked example of comparing a simple vs. complex grader's actual score lift.

Neither AIQUEST video gives quantitative accuracy/benchmark numbers beyond the vendors' own self-reported percentages (PDMD, DMAD, StoryMem) — no independent third-party validation of the claimed win rates or consistency scores is discussed.
StoryMem's actual generation speed/latency and GPU runtime are not covered in GM70MDyl94E — only parameter count, training-clip count, and VRAM footprint are given.

Cu8kUBwLoTM's '100x engineer' framing is entirely anecdotal — no controlled before/after task-timing data is given beyond rough verbal estimates ('a week or a month' vs 'an afternoon'), so the productivity multiplier can't be independently checked.
None of the videos address the legal/licensing risk of using AI to reverse-engineer vendor BIOS dumps, leaked drivers, or proprietary hardware docs (a theme Cu8kUBwLoTM raises but doesn't resolve).

No corpus content on how to measure or prove the '3 hours saved per analyst per week' success metric mentioned as the RAG project's definition of done — the demo build never gets tested with real analysts.
No discussion of exact pricing or contract terms for the LLM evals program/consulting beyond the sprint pricing given in Q679gH7oszg; the eval video doesn't connect its framework back to billing.
No detail on how the agency actually recruits, interviews, or onboards subcontractors mentioned in Q679gH7oszg beyond 'depending on the contracts' — the hiring process itself is not covered.
No concrete numbers on LLM API cost for the news aggregator or document-copilot projects beyond the single qF5il_9IwME remark about $1-2 per RAG query — no monthly cost estimate for either demo app.

The videos never show what the actual LLM-as-judge prompt looked like after iteration to reach high agreement, only the general meta-prompting technique — no worked example of a 'good' judge prompt verbatim.

No coverage of how Pydantic AI's tool-calling loop actually decides when to stop calling tools versus finalize an answer (the internal stopping criteria) — only that it 'decides' based on instructions.

No discussion of multi-tenant security hardening (RLS policy specifics, rate limiting, abuse prevention) beyond enabling Supabase row-level security by default — the videos don't show what a bad RLS policy misconfiguration looks like.
None of the four videos give concrete cost figures for running this stack in production (cloud bills, inference cost per token at scale, GPU rental cost for fine-tuning larger models).

No video explains how to decide, with real criteria, whether a given task should be solved with prompting/RAG, a sub-agent harness, LoRA fine-tuning, or full RL — each video touches part of this but none gives a unified decision framework.

The fine-tuning video (9LU90uI4WRU) doesn't cover how to evaluate a fine-tuned model beyond eyeballing one or two sample answers and the training loss number — no held-out test set or quantitative eval is shown.
Gaurav Sen's concept primer doesn't include any code or tool names, so a viewer still needs a separate hands-on tutorial to implement tokenization, RAG, or MCP.

Dave Ebbelaar's stack video doesn't address how to choose which specific LLM/provider to call for a given automation task, security/compliance concerns, or how to monitor the deployed system in production.
Vivek Trivedy's interview describes hooks, verification, and context-rot mitigations conceptually but gives no concrete code example of how a hook or virtual file system is implemented.
No video in this cluster addresses agent security, prompt-injection defenses, or guardrails for production agent deployments.
Neither eval-focused video gives a concrete numeric threshold (e.g. a specific match-rate or pass-rate percentage) for when a judge or agent is 'good enough' to ship to production.

The trading-bot and YouTube-automation videos never apply any observability/tracing to the Claude-built systems they ship, so there's no guidance on monitoring those bots for drift, silent MCP failures, or scheduled-job crashes once left running unattended.
No video discloses the ongoing cost of running an eval pipeline at scale (LangSmith/Arise pricing tiers, token costs of repeated LLM-as-judge calls) once you move past a 10-100 row golden dataset.

Ray Fu's trading-bot and YouTube videos show no actual outcome data (no real trading P&L, no verified channel revenue from his own content) — the dollar figures cited are projections or other creators' public subscriber/RPM numbers, not demonstrated results from the workflow itself.

The LangChain webinar openly admits its prompt-injection / security-eval use case is not yet built or demoed, leaving no concrete technique for applying agent observability to security detection today.

None of the four videos discusses what happens when the underlying automation fails partway (a scheduled bot missing its 9:30 EST run, an MCP disconnect, a sandbox/infra timeout flagged in Terminal-Bench) beyond noting that such errors exist.

None of the videos show the actual data-engineering code that turns raw transcripts/logs into prompt-response pairs for fine-tuning (v7qMjy_RxOs promises this for a future video in the series but doesn't demonstrate it here).

No video gives dollar-cost figures for any of the AI design tools (Claude, Grok, Codex, paper.design, Figma AI) or for fine-tuning hardware (RTX 5090, cloud GPU rental) — only time and token/VRAM counts are given.

The corpus doesn't address how to combine fine-tuning, RAG, and an agentic loop together in one production system — v7qMjy_RxOs presents them as a sequential decision tree, not a combined architecture.
No video benchmarks AMD ROCm or Nvidia's unified-memory "Spark" machines for fine-tuning in practice, despite both being mentioned as emerging options.

Neither design video explains how to measure or validate that an AI-assisted design actually passes accessibility/contrast checks in code (only Figma-level accessibility audits are covered, not shipped frontend code).

Sebastian Raschka's evaluation section doesn't say how to pick a good small-model-as-judge prompt beyond pointing to a reader-contributed GitHub discussion; no systematic guidance on validating a judge model against human ratings is given.
None of the videos discuss team/organizational rollout of these workflows at scale (e.g., onboarding a whole design or ML team to these AI practices) beyond individual-contributor tips.
